Scalp, Muscles of Facial Expression & Facial Nerve

The five layers of the scalp, every muscle of facial expression with its origin, insertion and action, the branches of CN VII, and the sensory map of the face.

Lecture 6 · Part 1The Scalp

Lecturer: Dr Nur Hassan, BDS, PGT (Oral Surg), PhD.

The five layers — SCALP

The layers spell the word, outer → inner
SkinConnective tissue (dense)Aponeurosis Loose connective tissuePericranium
LayerDescription
SkinThe thickest layer; contains hair, sebaceous and sweat glands; well vascularised
Connective tissue (dense)Heavily vascularised dense connective tissue; carries the artery, vein and nerve supply; bleeds profusely when cut
AponeurosisContains the occipitofrontalis muscle and the galea aponeurotica
Loose connective tissueThin, mobile, avascular
PericraniumPeriosteum of the cranium
Why scalping injuries happen: the first three layers — S, C and A — are bound tightly together and move as a single unit. The loose connective tissue beneath them is the natural cleavage plane, so the whole S-C-A block can be torn away together.
And why scalp wounds bleed so much: the vessels sit in the dense connective tissue layer, which holds them open when cut instead of letting them retract and constrict.

Neurovasculature of the scalp

Nerves — branches of CN V

  • Supratrochlear (V1)
  • Supraorbital (V1)
  • Zygomaticotemporal (V2)
  • Auriculotemporal (V3)

Nerves — cervical plexus

  • Greater auricular
  • Lesser occipital, C2–C3

Nerves — dorsal rami of cervical nerves

  • Greater occipital, C2
  • Third occipital, C3

Arteries — from the internal carotid

  • Supratrochlear artery
  • Supraorbital artery

Arteries — from the external carotid

  • Superficial temporal artery
  • Posterior auricular artery
  • Occipital artery

Veins accompany the arteries.

Pattern worth noticing: the front of the scalp is supplied by the internal carotid (via the ophthalmic artery) and innervated by the trigeminal nerve; the back is supplied by the external carotid and innervated by cervical nerves. The dividing line runs roughly between the ears.

Lecture 6 · Part 2Muscles of Facial Expression

General principles

  • All are innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII)
  • They insert into the skin — which is what allows them to move the face
  • There is no deep fascia along the face
The six groups
OrbitalNasalOral AuricularScalpNeck

Scalp group — occipitofrontalis & procerus

MuscleOriginInsertionAction
Occipitofrontalis (frontal belly)Galea aponeuroticaSkin and subcutaneous tissue of the eyebrows and noseElevates the eyebrows and skin over the root of the nose; wrinkles the forehead — surprise
Occipitofrontalis (occipital belly)Superior nuchal lineGalea aponeuroticaRetracts the scalp and increases the effectiveness of the frontal belly
ProcerusNasal bone and lateral nasal cartilageSkin of the lower forehead between the eyebrowsDepresses the medial end of the eyebrow; wrinkles skin over the dorsum of the nose — disdain

MuscleOriginInsertionAction

Corrugator supercilii & risorius

MuscleOriginInsertionAction
RisoriusFascia and superficial muscles over the masseterSkin over the corner of the mouthRetracts the corner of the mouth — smiling, laughing, grimacing
Corrugator superciliiMedial end of the superciliary archSkin above the supraorbital marginActs with orbicularis oculi to pull the eyebrows medially and inferiorly (squinting)
Buccinator is the odd one out. It is a muscle of facial expression supplied by CN VII, but it is functionally a muscle of mastication support — it keeps the bolus on the occlusal table. It is not one of the four muscles of mastication, and it is not supplied by V3.

Lecture 6 · Part 3Motor Supply — Facial Nerve (CN VII)

The five terminal branches, superior → inferior
TemporalZygomaticBuccal Marginal mandibularCervical
Mnemonic: Ten Zebras Bit My Carrot — Temporal, Zygomatic, Buccal, Marginal mandibular, Cervical.
BranchMuscles supplied
Posterior auricularOccipital belly of occipitofrontalis
TemporalFrontal belly of occipitofrontalis; superior part of orbicularis oculi; corrugator supercilii
ZygomaticInferior part of orbicularis oculi; may also innervate muscles served by the buccal branch
BuccalBuccinator; zygomaticus major and minor; levator anguli oris; levator labii superioris; superior part of orbicularis oris; levator labii superioris alaeque nasi; nasalis
Marginal mandibularRisorius; inferior part of orbicularis oris; depressor anguli oris; depressor labii inferioris; mentalis — and, per the lecture slide, stylohyoid and the posterior belly of digastric
CervicalPlatysma
Check this one against your textbook: the slide lists stylohyoid and the posterior belly of digastric under the marginal mandibular branch. In the standard description these two muscles are supplied by separate branches given off before the facial nerve enters the parotid gland and divides — the nerve to stylohyoid and the digastric branch, which arise alongside the posterior auricular nerve. Learn the slide’s version for the unit if that is what is examined, but know the conventional account too.

Lecture 6 · Part 4Arteries & Veins of the Face

  • All are branches of the external carotid artery
  • The facial artery is the major artery of the face
  • Also contributing: superficial temporal, posterior auricular and occipital arteries
  • Veins follow the arteries

Facial artery — course

  • Crosses the inferior border of the mandible at the medial border of masseter
  • Then ascends across the face diagonally
  • Terminates as the angular artery, lateral to the nose; it has many anastomoses
  • Supplies the face, pharynx, soft palate, tonsils, submandibular gland, lips and nose
Named branches on this slide
Ascending palatineTonsillarSubmental Inferior labialSuperior labialAngularDorsal nasal
Numbering discrepancy between your two lectures: this slide calls the facial artery the 3rd branch of the ECA, while the blood-supply lecture calls it the 4th. Both are used — counting every ECA branch in order gives 4th; counting only the anterior branches (superior thyroid, lingual, facial) gives 3rd. Safest answer: “4th branch overall, 3rd of the anterior branches”.

Lecture 6 · Part 5Sensory Innervation of the Face

The big picture: the face is trigeminal territory — V1 ophthalmic above the eye, V2 maxillary across the midface, V3 mandibular over the lower jaw (but not the angle). The angle of the mandible and the skin over it are supplied by the great auricular nerve from the cervical plexus.

Dental relevance: the mental nerve and infra-orbital nerve are the two you will anaesthetise most often, and the buccal nerve explains why an inferior alveolar block alone does not numb the buccal gingiva of the lower molars.

ClinicalBell’s Palsy

  • A form of facial paralysis resulting from dysfunction of cranial nerve VII
  • Causes an inability to control the facial muscles on the affected side

What the facial nerve controls — and therefore what is lost

  • Blinking, and opening and closing of the eyes
  • Smiling and frowning
  • Salivation
  • Lacrimation (production of tears)
  • Supply to the stapedius muscle — the stapes is the ear bone involved in hearing, so patients may also get hyperacusis
Key clinical distinction: in Bell’s palsy the whole side of the face is affected, including the forehead. In an upper motor neurone lesion (such as a stroke) the forehead is spared, because the frontal belly receives input from both cerebral hemispheres. If the patient can still wrinkle their forehead, suspect a stroke rather than Bell’s palsy.
Why the eye needs protecting: with orbicularis oculi paralysed the patient cannot blink or close the eye, so the cornea dries out. Eye care is a priority in management.
